passage:
Class 10 note, by Binita Sharma, sports teacher. Monday.
Last Friday a visiting runner spoke at assembly. He lost his sight at twenty and has since run marathons with a guide, holding a short rope between them. Most students clapped and forgot. Chinmay didn't. He stayed back and asked the runner three questions about training. This morning he was at the ground at six, running laps alone. He told me, "If he can do that without seeing, what's my excuse?" He looked almost shaken, in a good way. I've given him a beginner's training plan and paired him with the athletics captain. I'll also ask if he wants to volunteer as a guide runner at the district event next month.

qa.q: How did the visiting runner run with a guide?
qa.a: Holding a short rope between them.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he said, "what's my excuse?"
qa.a: He felt deeply moved and inspired, almost shaken, by the runner's story.

qa.q: What did Binita Sharma do next to support Chinmay?
qa.a: She gave him a beginner's training plan, paired him with the athletics captain and planned to offer him guide-running.

qa.q: How might the athletics captain see training with Chinmay?
qa.a: The captain may feel pleased to help a keen beginner, or a little curious about his sudden drive.

grounding: A teacher's note records a teenager deeply inspired by a visiting runner's story, and how she supported him.

passage:
Sunday night. Baljeet's diary.
Went to see Shreya Didi conduct the college choir at the gurdwara hall. Thirty voices, and she stood in front with just her hands. When she lifted them, everyone went silent. When she opened them, the sound came out like a wave. I had goosebumps on my arms for the whole second song. I didn't even know the words. On the bus home I kept thinking, I want to do something that makes people feel like that. Not maybe conducting. Maybe music, maybe teaching. Something that pulls people together. I asked Didi how she learned. She laughed and said, "Start by singing badly in the college choir." I'm going to the audition next month.

qa.q: How many voices were in the choir?
qa.a: Thirty voices.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel during the second song?
qa.a: Baljeet felt deeply moved and inspired, with goosebumps on both arms.

qa.q: What small step is Baljeet taking after the evening?
qa.a: Going to the choir audition next month, following Didi's advice to start by singing.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel hearing that Baljeet wants to do something similar?
qa.a: She would likely feel touched and happy to have inspired a younger cousin.

grounding: A teenager's diary records being deeply moved by watching an older cousin conduct a choir.

passage:
Thursday. Nilesh's diary.
Nirmala wore a yellow dupatta to tuition today. I noticed because I notice everything she does. She laughed at something Sir said and tucked her hair behind her ear, and I missed the entire trigonometry problem. I've written her name in the back of my maths notebook eleven times. I imagine us walking home together, talking about books, even though I don't know if she reads. I don't actually know much about her. I've spoken to her twice: once to borrow an eraser, once to say "bye." But in my head she's perfect. Maybe tomorrow I'll say something normal. Like "Did you get the homework?" Ugh. Even that feels terrifying.

qa.q: What colour was Nirmala's dupatta?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about talking to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nilesh feels intensely nervous and excited, even terrified of saying something simple.

qa.q: What could help Nilesh see Nirmala more realistically?
qa.a: Having ordinary conversations with her and getting to know her, rather than imagining her as perfect.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Nilesh?
qa.a: She probably sees Nilesh as a quiet classmate who once borrowed an eraser, unaware of the crush.

passage: In Sangli, Manoj, fifteen, took the long road home every day, past the flower stall where Urmila helped her aunt after school. He had never spoken to her. But he knew she wore a steel bangle, that she hummed while tying marigolds, and that she laughed with her head back. He'd decided she was kind, clever and brave. At night he wrote her name in the margin of his history notes, then scribbled over it. His friend Salim noticed the detour. "You'll ride past her till the board exams?" Manoj went red. "I'm just taking the long way." "Do you even know what she likes?" Manoj opened his mouth, then closed it. He didn't know a single thing she liked.

qa.q: What does Urmila hum while doing?
qa.a: While tying marigolds.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Salim asked if he knew what she liked?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit shaken, realising he knew almost nothing about her.

qa.q: What could Manoj do if he wants to know Urmila as a real person?
qa.a: He could start a simple, respectful conversation at the stall, and accept however she responds.

passage: The farewell dance list went up on the hostel noticeboard on Thursday. Simran, seventeen, had asked Varun to be her partner the week before. His name was next to Kritika's. Nobody had told her. She read it twice, then walked back to her room very carefully, as if she might break. Her roommate Dolma found her sitting on the floor with her back against the bed, not crying, just staring. "Simran?" "He said he'd think about it," Simran said. "I thought that meant yes." Then the tears came, hard. Dolma sat down beside her and put an arm around her. Later, Dolma brought her dinner from the mess and they watched a silly film on Dolma's laptop. Simran barely ate, but she stayed.

qa.q: Where did the farewell dance list go up?
qa.a: On the hostel noticeboard.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she walked back to her room very carefully?
qa.a: She felt shocked and deeply hurt, as if she might break.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Simran, held her, brought dinner and kept her company without pushing her to talk.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt finding Simran on the floor?
qa.a: Dolma probably felt worried and sad for her friend.

grounding: A hostel student processes the pain of romantic rejection with her roommate's support.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta Akka,
I know you're busy with your exams, so sorry for the long letter. Pooja stopped being my friend. Six years, Akka. Since Class 4. She's been sitting with the new girls, and yesterday I asked her if I did something wrong, and she said, "No, we've just grown apart." Like it was nothing. I came home and couldn't eat. I keep checking her status to see if she's sad too. She isn't. Everything reminds me of her: the swing, our walk to the bus. It feels like someone died, which is stupid, because nobody died. Amma says I'll make new friends. I told her it doesn't help. Can you call me on Sunday?
Keerthana

qa.q: How many years were Keerthana and Pooja friends?
qa.a: Six years.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel after Pooja's words?
qa.a: Keerthana feels heartbroken and overwhelmed, unable to eat and missing Pooja everywhere.

qa.q: What could help Keerthana through this?

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel worried and protective, wanting to call and comfort Keerthana.

grounding: A teenager writes to an older sister about the pain of a long friendship ending.

passage: "You asked what happened with me and Ananya, Ritu. I'm Vaibhav, and okay, here it is. She ended it by text. Two lines. 'I think we should just be friends. Sorry.' We'd been together four months. I read it in the school bus and just... kept reading it. I felt sick. I didn't cry in the bus, but I cried in the bathroom at home with the tap running so nobody would hear. For a week I didn't want to eat or play football. I kept thinking, what's wrong with me? My dad finally sat with me and said it happened to him at seventeen too. It helped, a bit. It still hurts. But I'm eating again. And I'm back at football on Tuesday."

passage:
"Arohi, can I tell you something?"
"Sure."
"You know how I always say I'm fine? That I don't care who I sit with?"
"Yeah, you're, like, the chillest person."
Ritu looked at her shoes. "I'm not. I eat lunch in the library because I don't know how to join people. I pretend to read."
Arohi was quiet.
"I've never told anyone. I thought if I said it, it'd be real."
"Ritu... I thought you liked being alone."
"I thought if I looked like I liked it, nobody would feel sorry for me."
Arohi slid closer. "Sit with me tomorrow. I'll save a place."
Ritu's eyes stung. "Promise you won't make it weird?"
"Promise," Arohi said, smiling. "Only a little weird."

qa.q: Where does Ritu eat lunch?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as she looked at her shoes?
qa.a: She felt nervous and exposed, taking the risk of revealing her loneliness.

qa.q: How did Arohi respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: Arohi listened quietly and then offered to save Ritu a seat, turning the confession into a real step.

qa.q: How does Arohi's view of Ritu change?
qa.a: Arohi had thought Ritu liked being alone and now understands she was lonely and hiding it.

grounding: A teenager takes the risk of admitting her loneliness to a classmate.

passage: I'm Farida. Last year, before the science olympiad, everyone thought I was calm. I kept saying, "It's just a test." But I'd been waking up at three in the morning, heart racing, sure I'd let everyone down. One evening, sitting on the steps with Ira, I finally said it. "I'm scared I'm not as smart as people think." My voice went strange. I was waiting for her to laugh or to say, "Don't be silly." She didn't. She said, "I feel like that every time I paint." Then we just sat there. It didn't fix anything. But the next time I woke up at three, I texted her, and she replied a thumbs-up at seven, and somehow that was enough.

qa.q: What time was Farida waking up?
qa.a: At three in the morning.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when finally telling Ira the truth?
qa.a: Farida felt scared and exposed, voice going strange, expecting to be laughed at.

qa.q: What did Ira's reply do that helped?
qa.a: It met Farida's honesty with her own, so Farida felt less alone instead of judged.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt when Farida opened up?
qa.a: Ira may have felt trusted and moved, and safe enough to share her own worry.

grounding: A teenager recalls the risk of admitting to a friend the fear of not being smart enough.

passage:
Counsellor's note, peer support circle, Class 11. Vijay Rao.
Today's circle was on "what we hide." Most students shared small things. Then Gargi, who usually passes, raised her hand. She said her parents think she wants to be a doctor, and she has never told them she wants to study design, because she's scared they'll be disappointed in her. Her voice shook and she didn't look up. The room went quiet. One boy said, "Me too, but engineering." She laughed and cried at the same time. I thanked her for trusting the group. After the circle, I asked if she'd like help planning a conversation with her parents. She said yes. We meet on Thursday.

qa.q: What does Gargi want to study?
qa.a: Design.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when her voice shook?

passage: "The school magazine asked how I handle board stress, so okay. I'm Elizabeth, Class 12. In January I was a mess. I couldn't sleep, my stomach hurt before every mock, I snapped at my mum. Coach Yogesh noticed I'd stopped coming to the track. He said, 'Come back for twenty minutes. Just run.' So I did. Every evening, twenty minutes, even in revision week. Then I added one thing: before each paper, I stand with my feet flat and breathe out longer than I breathe in. Sounds tiny. But my shoulders come down. I still get nervous. The difference is now I know what to do with it. And I sleep."

qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel in January?

passage: I'm Zeenat, and I sat behind Ojas in the exam hall on Monday. Before the paper came, I saw his leg jiggling so fast the bench shook. His face was pale. Then he did something odd. He put both feet flat on the floor, pressed his palms together hard, and breathed out slowly, like blowing through a straw. Four or five times. Then he rolled his shoulders back. His leg stopped. When the paper came, he read it without rushing. Afterwards I asked him about it. He said the school counsellor taught him, and that it doesn't make the fear disappear, just smaller. I don't know how he really felt inside, but he looked calm enough to write.

passage: At the Lucknow school, the rule was simple: girls had to stay inside the campus until 5 p.m. for "safety," boys could leave at 3:30. Yusuf, sixteen, had never thought about it. Then Parul, his project partner, missed their library session because she wasn't allowed out. "Why are boys safe at 3:30 and girls aren't?" she asked. Yusuf opened his mouth to defend it, then couldn't. That evening he kept turning it over. If the roads were unsafe, weren't they unsafe for everyone? Was keeping girls in actually protecting them, or just easier for the school? The next day, he and Parul drafted a letter to the principal suggesting the same time for all, plus a teacher on duty at the gate. His hands were sweating when he signed it.

qa.q: At what time could boys leave the campus?
What was Yusuf feeling as he signed the letter?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with sweating hands, but committed to what he now believed was fair.

qa.q: What did Yusuf and Parul suggest, and why is it a reasonable approach?
qa.a: The same leaving time for all plus a teacher at the gate; it addresses safety without treating girls differently.

qa.q: How might the principal see the letter?
qa.a: The principal may feel challenged or defensive, or may appreciate the students' respectful suggestion.

grounding: A teenager questions a school rule that treats girls and boys differently and works to change it.

passage:
"Nikita Didi, is it wrong to lie if it helps someone?"
"Depends. What happened?"
"Sana's parents think she was at my house on Saturday. She wasn't. She went to see a film with her cousin. Her mum called me and I said yes, she was here."
"Why?"
"Because Sana begged me. And her parents are really strict."
"How do you feel now?"
Gargi pulled her knees up. "Bad. But also like I was being a good friend?"
"Both can be true."
"But which one matters more? Honesty or loyalty?"
Nikita thought. "Maybe the question is: what would you want if you were her mum?"
Gargi was silent a long time. "I'd want the truth. I'll tell Sana I can't cover again."

qa.q: Where was Sana really on Saturday?
qa.a: At a film with her cousin.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after lying to Sana's mum?
qa.a: Gargi felt guilty and torn, unsure whether being loyal made it right.

qa.q: What did Nikita's question help Gargi decide?
qa.a: To tell Sana she won't cover again, after imagining what she'd want as Sana's mum.

qa.q: How might Sana react when Gargi says she can't cover again?
qa.a: Sana might feel let down or annoyed at first, but may understand Gargi's reasons.

passage: I'm Farida. When I was fourteen, I noticed that in our building, Shanta Tai, who cleaned our flats, always took the stairs, all nine floors, even with buckets. I asked my mother why. "That's the rule," she said. "Lift is for residents." I couldn't stop thinking about it. It was the same lift and the same building. What made her different? I asked my friend Karthik, and he'd never noticed either. We went to the committee meeting together. My heart was pounding. I asked, "Who made this rule, and why?" Nobody had a good answer. It took three meetings, but the rule changed. Now when I see Shanta Tai in the lift, I feel something like pride, and also shame that I didn't ask sooner.

qa.q: How many floors did Shanta Tai climb?
qa.a: Nine floors.

qa.q: How did Farida feel after seeing Shanta Tai in the lift?
qa.a: Farida feels proud of changing the rule, but also ashamed of not asking sooner.

qa.q: What worked in how Farida challenged the rule?
qa.a: Asking plainly who made it and why, going with Karthik to the committee and persisting for three meetings.

qa.q: What is it like for Shanta Tai now, compared to before?
qa.a: She no longer has to climb nine floors with buckets, which is likely a real relief.

grounding: A person looks back on questioning a building rule that barred a cleaner from the lift, and getting it changed.

passage: Preeti Maasi tapped Arohi's hand. "When I was fifteen, a new girl, Kamla, joined our class from a village near Bikaner. She spoke with a thick accent, and the popular girls copied it every time she answered. Everyone laughed, even me, the first week. One day they took her notebook and read out her spelling mistakes. I felt sick. I stood up and said, 'Give it back. That's enough.' My hands were shaking. The room went dead quiet. Then I told our class teacher at lunch, and she spoke to the whole class that afternoon. The popular girls didn't talk to me for two months. But Kamla sat with me after that, and she became my closest friend." Arohi asked, "Were you scared?" "Very. I still did it."

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Preeti's story, and what did she do after standing up?

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when Preeti stood up for her?
qa.a: Kamla likely felt relieved and less alone, which is why they became close friends.

passage: The school bus was crammed and noisy after the Friday match, and the teacher on duty was sitting up front. At the back, two seniors had taken Jaya's bag, a Class 8 student, and were tossing it over her head while she tried to grab it. "Come on, jump!" People laughed. passage: At the Dadar coaching centre, a group of boys in the back row started imitating Pallavi's stammer whenever she answered. "W-w-well, Sir..." Some girls giggled. Urmila, sixteen, sat two rows away. Last week she had laughed along, quietly, and hated herself for it. Today Pallavi went silent halfway through an answer, her ears red. Urmila turned around. At the break, she sat next to Pallavi, and after class, she told the centre head exactly what had happened. The head called the boys in that evening. On the way out, Pallavi squeezed Urmila's hand without saying anything.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when her voice shook?

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Urmila spoke up?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and grateful, shown by her silent hand squeeze. 🤍

grounding: A teenager defends a classmate mocked for her stammer and reports it, despite the social risk.

passage:
Nature camp note, Night 3. Irfan Qureshi, camp mentor.
After the campfire, Ayesha, fifteen, stayed out on the rock looking at the stars. When I checked on her, she asked, "Do you think we're here for a reason, or is it just chance?" I asked what she thought. She said sometimes she feels part of everything, the trees, the people back home, even the stars, and other times she feels tiny and pointless. We talked for twenty minutes about how different traditions and thinkers answer that question. She said she'd been reading both her grandfather's Sufi poems and a science book on the universe, and they didn't feel as far apart as she expected. I suggested she keep a notebook of her questions. She has already started.

qa.q: On which night of camp did this happen?
qa.a: Night 3.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling as she looked at the stars?
qa.a: She felt a mix of wonder and connection, and also a sense of being tiny.

qa.q: What did Irfan Qureshi suggest, and why is it a good idea?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook of her questions, so she can explore them over time without needing quick answers.

qa.q: How might Irfan Qureshi have felt being asked such a big question?
qa.a: He likely felt moved and respectful, taking care not to give her a ready-made answer.

grounding: A camp mentor's note records a teenager exploring questions of existence, connection and meaning.

passage:
Tuesday. Parul's diary.
I sat with Anand Dadu on the terrace after dinner. He's eighty-one. I asked him what he thinks life is for. I thought he'd say something from the scriptures. He said, "For a long time I thought it was to earn and build. Now I think it's to be useful to someone, and to notice things." Then he pointed at the moon and said nothing for five minutes. I kept thinking about it in bed. What would I be useful for? What do I notice? I think I notice people who are left out. Maybe that's a start. It's weird: I felt small and big at the same time.

qa.q: How old is Anand Dadu?
qa.a: Eighty-one.

qa.q: How did Parul feel lying in bed after the talk?
qa.a: Parul felt thoughtful and moved, both small and big at the same time.

passage: In Malmö, the new boy, Yosef, had arrived from Syria in September and still spoke little Swedish. Some of the class mimicked his accent. Lars, sixteen, had laughed once, then felt uncomfortable about it for days. In October he asked his teacher if he could start a homework club at the library on Wednesdays, open to anyone learning Swedish. Four students came the first week, including Yosef. Lars explained grammar badly and Yosef corrected his maths. When a classmate sneered at them in the corridor, Lars said, "He's in my club. Leave it." His voice wobbled, but he held his ground. By December, twelve students came every week, and Lars had given up two afternoons of football for it.

qa.q: On which day did the homework club meet?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: How did Lars feel after laughing at Yosef once?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and guilty for days.

qa.q: What was effective about Lars's response, and how could the school support it?
qa.a: He turned his guilt into a club that helped many students; the school could give the club a teacher and a regular room.

qa.q: How might Yosef see the club and Lars's defence in the corridor?
qa.a: Yosef likely feels welcomed and less alone, with a place where his skills are valued.

grounding: A Swedish teenager starts a homework club for newcomer students and stands up for a mocked classmate.

passage: At the community centre in Dharavi, Joseph, seventeen, arrived every Saturday at nine to teach reading to a group of eight-year-olds. The coordinator, Tejas, had warned him the kids were restless. The first week, they ignored him. The second week, a boy threw a book. Joseph went home frustrated and nearly quit. But he came back with picture cards and let each child choose a story. By week five, the kids were waiting at the door. One girl read a whole page aloud and looked at him, beaming. Joseph felt a warmth in his chest he couldn't explain. "I'll take the Tuesday group too," he told Tejas. "If you need someone."

qa.q: At what time did Joseph arrive every Saturday?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after the second week?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and discouraged, nearly quitting.

qa.q: What change helped Joseph connect with the children?
qa.a: Bringing picture cards and letting each child choose a story.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Joseph offering to take the Tuesday group too?
qa.a: Tejas would likely be pleased and grateful to have such a committed volunteer.

grounding: A teenager finds meaning in volunteering to teach reading at a community centre despite a rough start.

passage: Rafiq Chacha stirred his tea slowly. "Kamal, when I was sixteen, my friends and I had new bikes. One evening on the highway, Irshad shouted, 'Race to the toll booth! Loser buys tea!' Everyone revved. My heart was pounding, my blood was hot, and I wanted to win so badly. Then I saw the truck in front and remembered my Abba saying, 'When you're excited, count to five before you act.' I counted. One, two, three... and I let them go. I rode slowly to the toll booth. Irshad got there first, and he had skidded and scraped his whole leg. He could have been worse. I paid for the tea anyway." Kamal grinned. "You lost, then." "I lost the race," Chacha said. "Nothing else."

qa.q: Where did Irshad want to race to?
qa.a: To the toll booth.

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when Irshad shouted "Race"?
qa.a: He felt excited and pumped up, heart pounding and wanting badly to win.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Rafiq's story?
qa.a: Seeing the truck and remembering his father's rule to count to five before acting when excited.

qa.q: How might Irshad have felt after scraping his leg?
qa.a: He was probably shaken and in pain, and may have regretted starting the race.

grounding: An uncle remembers counting to five to calm down during a peer-pressured bike race as a teenager.

passage: It was 11 p.m., the night before the chemistry exam, and Sabina's phone was at nine percent. Then she saw the group chat: Nandini had posted a photo from the party Sabina wasn't invited to. Her face went hot. She typed fast: "Wow, thanks for inviting me, fake friends. Hope you had fun." Her thumb hovered over send. The screen dimmed. She called Nandini instead, but Nandini didn't answer. Sabina put the phone down, breathing hard. She reread her message. In the morning, would she still mean it? She deleted it and wrote in her notebook instead: "Ask N tomorrow, calmly." She plugged in her phone and opened the chemistry book, though her hands were still trembling.

qa.q: What percentage was Sabina's phone at?
qa.a: Nine percent.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she typed the message?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, left out of the party.

qa.q: What helped Sabina avoid sending the angry message?
qa.a: Pausing, rereading it and asking herself if she'd still mean it in the morning, then writing a calmer plan.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel if she had received the angry message?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and defensive, making it harder to sort things out.

grounding: A teenager stops herself from sending an angry message in the heat of the moment the night before an exam.

passage: After the birthday party in Kochi, it was nearly ten, and Jomon, sixteen, stood by the gate with three friends and one scooter. "Triple seat, come on! It's two kilometres," said Arun, already on it. Everyone was laughing, loud, still buzzing from the music. Jomon felt the pull. It would take five minutes. Nobody would know. But he saw the dark road, no streetlights, and remembered his sister Lakshmi's friend who fell off a scooter last year. He stepped back. "I'll call Lakshmi Chechi to pick me up." Arun groaned. "Seriously?" "Seriously." Jomon called. Lakshmi came in ten minutes. In the car he said nothing for a while, then, "They thought I was boring." Lakshmi squeezed his shoulder. "Boring gets home."

qa.q: How far was the ride, according to Arun?
qa.a: Two kilometres.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he felt the pull to get on the scooter?
qa.a: He felt excited and tempted by the fun and the group, but uneasy about the dark road.

qa.q: What helped Jomon make a cooler-headed choice?
qa.a: Pausing to picture the dark road and his sister's friend's fall, and calling Lakshmi instead.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Jomon called her?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and proud that he chose safety over pressure.

grounding: A teenager resists peer pressure to ride triple on a scooter at night by calling his sister.
